[NASA Glenn Combustion Science Overview]: Explore Combustion Science being performed at Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio.

In the United States, combustion processes contribute to about 85% of delivered energy and are an integral part in many industrial fabrication processes. Combustion produces greenhouse gases and soot, which contributes to global warming and causes significant health concerns. The Combustion Science Discipline conducts idealized experiments on the International Space Station where the removal of gravity enables researchers to study details of the combustion processes that cannot be readily studied on the ground. The Space Station environment also provides an important test-bed for studying spacecraft fire risk.

Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. For

[NASA Glenn Combustion Science Overview]: the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture). These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury contamination from coal, and wild-land fires).

[NASA Glenn Combustion Science Overview]: e analyses. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one-dimensional systems.

To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300 degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter. The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward. The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. Figure 1 contains a gallery of 1-g to 0-g comparison flames.

FM2 is the first-ever combustion experiment to be performed on another planetary body. Building on the success of the decades-long combustion science ground (1g) program and International Space Station (ISS) microgravity (~0g) combustion experiment campaigns, FM2 investigates burning materials on the Moon at its 1/6 reduced gravity level.

The Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) investigation examines the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples in microgravity.

The Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed to ensure that a modified P-Trak—a key component of the forthcoming NASA Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)—will perform properly in the unique environment of microgravity.

The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) experiment was designed to assess and quantify the effectiveness of inert-gas suppressants in microgravity and obtain the most conservative estimate of the limiting oxygen index for steady combustion.

Creating a safe environment for astronauts is the number one priority

The CIR’s main feature is a 100-liter combustion chamber to provide the necessary safety features necessary for the various combustion investigations and is the only rack on ISS dedicated to combustion experimentation. Developed by NASA’s Glenn Research Center, the CIR was launched to the International Space Station (ISS) in November 2008 by the Space Shuttle (STS-126).

source_pdf: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir
text:
[25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir]: On Feb. 24, 1997, the six crew members aboard the Russian space station Mir faced significant danger when a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system. The searing flame, lasting several minutes, not only cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles but also filled the station’s modules with smoke. Although the narrow confines where the fire occurred made fighting it difficult, through teamwork and composure the crew prevailed and extinguished the flames, with no damage to the station’s structure. The station’s life support systems cleared its atmosphere of the toxic smoke over several hours, with no lasting harm to the crew members. The lessons learned from the incident were passed on in the design and operations of the International Space Station.

source_pdf: NASA Spinoff: Fire Detector (Smoke vs Dust Discrimination)
text: [NASA Spinoff: Fire Detector (Smoke vs Dust Discrimination)]: Because the liquid hydrogen which NASA stores for the space shuttle engines is easily ignited, a hand held ultraviolet fire detector was developed by detector electronics under NASA contract. The system was commercialized by Detector Electronics for use in other hydrogen handling facilities. The detector sensors spot a hydrogen flame at 100 feet, show radiation levels and provide an aural fire alert.

[NASA Spinoff: Fireman's Air Tanks]: Together with NASA's Johnson Space Center, A-T-O Inc.'s Scott Aviation has developed light-weight firefighter's air tanks.  New backpack system weighs only 20 pounds for 30 minute air supply, 13 pounds less than conventional firefighting tanks. They are pressurized at 4,500 psi, (twice current tanks). Made of aluminum liner wrapped by resin-impregnated glass fibers, eliminating corrosion as well as lightening the load. Redesigned face mask permits better vision. Warning device to tell fireman he is running out of air is personalized so it can't be heard by others reducing confusion in an already hectic environment.  Structural Composites Inc., The Boeing Co., and Martin-Marietta Corp. have developed uses for this technology.

text: [NASA Spinoff: New Technology for the Fire Attire]: Although little can be done to reduce the risks of firefighting, something can be done to curb the injuries and fatalities. This is the goal of Project FIRES, a program jointly sponsored by NASA and the Federal Emergency Management Agency's U.S. Fire Administration with technical management provided by Marshall Space Flight Center. Project FIRES (Firefighter's Integrated Response Equipment System) involves applications of advanced materials and design concepts, derived from Apollo to update existing gear which does not adequately protect against many of the hazards encountered in fire suppression activities. A major focus of the effort involves application to the FIRES ensemble of lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials originally developed for use in astronauts' space suits

[ISS_Combustion_Researcher_Guide.pdf - Trang 8]: 8 Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture). These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury contamination from coal, and wild-land fires). Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact on human health, comfort and safety. Conclusion The Saffire series of experiment provides the unique opportunity to address gaps in knowledge and capabilities regarding fire safety aboard spacecraft. The Saffire-I, II, and III flight systems will address large-scale flame spread and material flammability limits, both essential components of understanding fire behavior and quantifying fire risks aboard spacecraft. Continuing these investigations and addressing other knowledge gaps will require a more ambitious experiment in Saffire-IV-VI but, by simulating a more complete fire response scenario and demonstrating post-fire monitoring and cleanup capabilities, these experiments will significantly improve crew safety on all future exploration missions. The minimum in the flammability boundary is at very low flows, on the order of diffusive flows. This minimum occurs where the flow still permits enough heat release to sustain the flame but not so strong that it sweeps the fuel out of the hot flame zone before it can react. As ambient O2 is reduced, flame temperatures are reduced, which slows down the reaction time. Thus the flow needed to blow off the flame becomes slower as oxygen decreases and the flame temperature is reduced. (Stretch rate = 3/2 U/R) Flame image very near the bottom of the flammability curve. Near the rod tip the flame is strongest. The rod is blackened at the tip, and there is a clear bubble layer that extends along the rod to the downstream edge of the flame. Beyond that, there are a few bubbles, but not the dense bubbles in the layer beneath the flame.

[PSI-26_BASS_NTRS_20160000593.pdf - Trang 19]: Spacecraft Materials Microgravity Research on Flammability PMMA flammability boundary. The minimum in the flammability boundary is at very low flows, on the order of diffusive flows. This minimum occurs where the flow still permits enough heat release to sustain the flame but not so strong that it sweeps the fuel out of the hot flame zone before it can react. As ambient O2 is reduced, flame temperatures are reduced, which slows down the reaction time. Thus the flow needed to blow off the flame becomes slower as oxygen decreases and the flame temperature is reduced. (Stretch rate = 3/2 U/R) Flame image very near the bottom of the flammability curve. Near the rod tip the flame is strongest. The rod is blackened at the tip, and there is a clear bubble layer that extends along the rod to the downstream edge of the flame. Beyond that, there are a few bubbles, but not the dense bubbles in the layer beneath the flame.

[PSI-26_BASS_NTRS_20210011385.pdf - Trang 2]: NASA STI Program . . . in Profile Since its founding, NASA has been dedicated to the advancement of aeronautics and space science. The NASA Scientific and Technical Information (STI) Program plays a key part in helping NASA maintain this important role. The NASA STI Program operates under the auspices of the Agency Chief Information Officer. It collects, organizes, provides for archiving, and disseminates NASA’s STI. Conclusion The Saffire series of experiment provides the unique opportunity to address gaps in knowledge and capabilities regarding fire safety aboard spacecraft. The Saffire-I, II, and III flight systems will address large-scale flame spread and material flammability limits, both essential components of understanding fire behavior and quantifying fire risks aboard spacecraft. Continuing these investigations and addressing other knowledge gaps will require a more ambitious experiment in Saffire-IV-VI but, by simulating a more complete fire response scenario and demonstrating post-fire monitoring and cleanup capabilities, these experiments will significantly improve crew safety on all future exploration missions. If a material passes this test, then it is considered safe for spaceflight. This test has been a practical means to assess the great number of materials that have been screened. However, microgravity research has suggested that normal gravity may not represent the most flammable condition for a material. Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g). Flame Spread in Microgravity over 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL Fabric. Left: Concurrent flow (comparable to 1-g upward spread). Right: Opposed flow (comparable to 1-g downward spread). In microgravity, both concurrent and opposed-flow flame spread are possible, but on Earth, downward flame spread (opposed flow) cannot be achieved. This demonstrates enhanced flammability in microgravity, and suggests similar behavior at partial gravity.

[FUTURE-LUCI-FM2_LUCI & FM2 (Upcoming)_NTRS_20210020516.pdf - Trang 10]: Page 10 Proposed Concept: Overview We propose to use a small chamber to conduct the first-ever combustion tests on another world. Hypothesis: some materials burning in Lunar-g are more flammable than on Earth. This has important implications for the current 1-g material screening method used by NASA. Four fuel samples individually burned in Lunar gravity; Cameras and other sensors record flame characteristics. Oxygen limits for upward and downward spread on the Moon will be compared to 1-g values. Measured flame characteristics in 1-g and Lunar-g will be compared to detailed model predictions. These comparisons will refine pressure-gravity scaling relations and will be applied to other g-levels. The work directly addresses knowledge gaps in flammability and crew safety as defined in several NASA strategic documents.

BASS-II (PSI-25 - Burning and Suppression of Solids - II): Đốt vật liệu rắn (vải, nhựa PMMA) trong ống gió quạt thuộc tủ MSG. Chứng minh luồng gió tốc độ thấp (3-10 cm/s) trong 0g làm vật liệu cháy mạnh hơn và hạ ngưỡng oxy tối thiểu (LOC) xuống thấp hơn so với trên Trái Đất. Nhiên liệu: Sibal fabric (cotton-fiberglass), PMMA acrylic slabs/rods, Nomex.

BASS (PSI-26 - Burning and Suppression of Solids): Thí nghiệm nền tảng khảo sát tốc độ cháy lan ngược dòng và xuôi dòng gió cưỡng bức cũng như dập lửa bằng dòng khí Nitơ trong tủ MSG. Nhiên liệu: Solid polymer rods, thin films, cotton-fiberglass.

SAFFIRE-I (PSI-98 - Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment - I): Đốt tấm vải Sibal kích thước lớn (0.4 x 0.94 m) trên tàu chở hàng Cygnus sau khi rời ISS để đo giới hạn phát triển đám cháy quy mô thật. Nhiên liệu: Large Sibal cloth (0.4 m x 0.94 m, 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass).

SAFFIRE-II (PSI-99 - Spacecraft Fire Experiment - II): Thử nghiệm 9 mẫu vật liệu tàu vũ trụ (Sibal, Silicone, PMMA dày/mỏng, Nomex) ở tốc độ gió 20 và 30 cm/s để kiểm chứng tiêu chuẩn NASA-STD-6001 trong 0g. Nhiên liệu: 9 samples (5 cm x 29 cm): Sibal, Silicone, structured PMMA, flat PMMA, Nomex.

SAFFIRE-III (PSI-100 - Spacecraft Fire Experiment - III): Đốt mẫu quy mô lớn ở bầu khí quyển mô phỏng Căn cứ Mặt Trăng / tàu thám hiểm (tăng nồng độ O2, giảm áp suất xuống ~10.2 psi). Nhiên liệu: Large Sibal cotton-fiberglass panel at exploration atmosphere.

ACME-CFI-G (PSI-159 - ACME Cool Flames Investigation with Gases): Thí nghiệm có nồng độ Oxy cao nhất trên PSI (lên tới 85% O2 từ đầu đốt cầu tạo ngọn lửa đảo ngược inside-out), tạo ra ngọn lửa lạnh khuếch tán ổn định ở 500-1000 K. Nhiên liệu: Propane, n-Butane, n-Pentane (Spherical porous burner, normal & inverse inside-out flames).

ACME-FlameDesign (PSI-10 - ACME Flame Design - Spherical Diffusion Flames): Khảo sát sự hình thành bồ hóng (soot) và giới hạn tắt lửa do bức xạ nhiệt của ngọn lửa cầu trong buồng CIR. Nhiên liệu: Ethylene, Methane spherical diffusion flames.

SPICE (PSI-107 - Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment): Xác định điểm sinh khói (smoke point) khi ngọn lửa khí bắt đầu phát thải muội than trong ống gió quạt thuộc tủ MSG. Nhiên liệu: Ethylene, Propane, Methane, Propylene in co-flowing air.

ACME-BRE (ACME-BRE - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME Project)): Dùng đầu đốt khí phẳng bằng đồng xốp trong buồng CIR để giả lập tốc độ hóa hơi và khả năng cháy của vật liệu rắn/lỏng trong môi trường tĩnh (still atmosphere). Nhiên liệu: Ethylene/Methane doped with N2/CO2 simulating PMMA, Delrin, paper, alcohols.

SLICE (MSG-SLICE - Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment): Dùng chung ống gió quạt SPICE với BASS trong tủ MSG để đo cấu trúc chân ngọn lửa và hiện tượng nhấc lửa (liftoff) cho tới khi bị thổi tắt. Nhiên liệu: Methane co-flow laminar jet flames.

SAME (PSI-102 - Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment): Chứng minh hạt khói trong vi trọng lực kết tụ thành kích thước lớn hơn so với 1g do thiếu đối lưu tự nhiên, làm thay đổi độ nhạy của đầu báo khói quang học và ion hóa. Nhiên liệu: Overheated spacecraft materials: Kapton, Teflon, Silicone, Cellulose, Lampwick.

SAME-R (PSI-101 - Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight): Mở rộng dữ liệu phân bố kích thước hạt khói theo thời gian lão hóa (aging time) để hiệu chuẩn đầu báo cháy thế hệ mới cho tàu Orion và căn cứ Mặt Trăng. Nhiên liệu: 66 test points of pyrolyzed spacecraft wiring and insulation materials.

DAFT & DAFT-2 (MSG-DAFT - Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test): Dùng chung máy đo hạt của thí nghiệm khói SAME/SAME-R để đo đặc trưng bụi lơ lửng, giúp thiết kế đầu báo cháy phân biệt khói thật và bụi Mặt Trăng (tránh báo động giả như trên Artemis II). Nhiên liệu: Cabin dust & Lunar regolith simulant aerosols.

FLEX (PSI-69 - Flame Extinguishment Experiment): Gồm 275 lần đốt giọt nhiên liệu lỏng trong thiết bị MDCA (tủ CIR) nhằm đo nồng độ CO2 và Helium tối thiểu để dập tắt lửa trong không gian. Nhiên liệu: Methanol, n-Heptane droplets (1.5 - 4.0 mm) with CO2, He, N2 diluents.

FLEX-2 (PSI-68 - Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 & Cool Flames (CFI)): Phát hiện hiện tượng giọt nhiên liệu sau khi tắt lửa nóng vẫn tiếp tục cháy âm ỉ ở chế độ Ngọn lửa lạnh (Cool Flame) vô hình và có thể tự bùng cháy lại. Nhiên liệu: n-Heptane, n-Octane, n-Decane, Iso-octane droplets & arrays.

Cool-Flames-Model (PSI-142 - Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions (FLEX Derivative)): Tổng hợp dữ liệu chuyển tiếp giữa ngọn lửa nóng và ngọn lửa lạnh phục vụ mô hình hóa dự báo cháy lại sau khi phun chất chữa cháy. Nhiên liệu: Higher n-alkanes and multicomponent fuels.

ACME-E-FIELD (ACME-E-FIELD - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames): GIẢ LẬP TRỌNG LỰC MẶT TRĂNG & SAO HỎA: Dùng lực điện trường đẩy các ion tự nhiên trong ngọn lửa để tái tạo hiệu ứng đối lưu nổi tương đương trọng lực từng phần (0.16g - 0.38g). Nhiên liệu: Methane/Ethylene flames under high-voltage electric field (up to 10 kV).

LUCI & FM2 (Upcoming) (FUTURE-LUCI-FM2 - Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) & Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)): [DATA GAP TRÊN PSI]: Hiện chưa có dữ liệu cháy ở trọng lực từng phần (0.16g Mặt Trăng) trên PSI. Cần dùng kết quả 0g (BASS-II, Saffire-III, CFI-G) kết hợp 1g và giả lập điện trường E-FIELD để nội suy giới hạn an toàn. Nhiên liệu: Spacecraft & Moon Base fabrics/polymers at >=30% O2, <=10.2 psi, 0.16g.
